title: Most models miss SNAP's minimum benefit when broad-based categorical eligibility lifts the income limits
paragraphs: Most of the {nModels} models on PolicyBench answer $0 for {householdCount} households that qualify for SNAP food benefits. A $0 answer could keep someone who qualifies from applying. PolicyEngine puts the correct amount for each household at SNAP's minimum benefit, ${minimumMonthly} a month or ${referenceAmount} for 2026, and each qualifies for it only through broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE). Of the {answers} answers PolicyBench requests for these households, {zeroAnswers} come to $0 and {hits} match the correct amount.

Each household fails an ordinary SNAP income test that BBCE lifts in its state. A Michigan worker who pays child support has gross income above SNAP's ordinary limit of {snapGrossLimit}% of the federal poverty guideline, as does a {txAge}-year-old in Texas with wages and ${financialAssistance} of financial assistance. A Connecticut couple on Social Security disability income, a disabled Michigan resident living alone, and an {wiAge}-year-old surviving spouse in Wisconsin fail SNAP's ordinary net income test. The Connecticut couple also holds ${ctSavings} in savings, above SNAP's asset limit. Under BBCE, a state extends SNAP to households eligible for a non-cash benefit funded by Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF). Connecticut, Michigan, and Wisconsin set that benefit's gross income limit at {bbceGrossLimitHigh}% of the guideline and Texas at {bbceGrossLimitTx}%, none of them applies a net income test, and only Texas keeps an asset limit. All {householdCount} households fall under their state's gross limit, and at their incomes SNAP's regular formula pays nothing, so each gets the minimum.

When savings rather than income stand in the way, most models answer above $0. PolicyBench also asks models about households in New Jersey, North Carolina, Virginia, and Pennsylvania that pass SNAP's income tests but hold savings above its asset limit, which BBCE removes in those states. For those {assetOnlyCount} households, {assetOnlyAbove0Share}% of answers come in above $0, against {fiveAbove0Share}% for the {householdCount} above the ordinary income limits. GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5.1 answer above $0 for each household held back by savings and $0 for each of the {householdCount}. Models name categorical eligibility in {assetOnlyBbceMentions} of their {assetOnlyExplanations} explanations for the households held back by savings, and {assetOnlyBbceAssets} of those also mention assets. For the {householdCount} above the ordinary income limits, {fiveBbceMentions} of {explanations} explanations name it, and {fiveBbceZeros} of them still end at $0. Of those {fiveBbceZeros}, {fiveBbceZeroWithNetLimit} cite a net income limit that none of the households' states applies under BBCE.

GPT-6 Astra gets the most of these households right, {astraHits} of {householdCount}, each time citing the state's {bbceGrossLimitHigh}%-of-poverty limit for categorical eligibility. It answers $0 for the Texas resident and the Michigan worker, whose gross incomes exceed SNAP's ordinary limit. Claude Opus 5.5 answers ${opusOn108} for the Wisconsin surviving spouse, citing Wisconsin's BBCE and its {bbceGrossLimitHigh}% limit. For the Connecticut couple and the disabled Michigan resident it answers $0, citing SNAP's ordinary net income limit, which BBCE removes in both states. GPT-6 Sol, which leads PolicyBench overall, answers $0 for {sol6ZeroCount} of the {householdCount} and names categorical eligibility in {sol6BbceMentions} of its SNAP explanations across all {boardHouseholds} households. For the Texas resident, GPT-6 Sol answers ${sol6On030} and Claude Opus 5.5 answers ${opusOn030}, and both compute a regular benefit from wages alone. PolicyEngine also counts the ${financialAssistance} of financial assistance as income, which puts the household above SNAP's ordinary limits and leaves BBCE as its only route. The prompt labels that money only "financial assistance", so both answers turn on what counts as income, not on BBCE.

The prompt tells every model to treat any "unlisted household fact, boolean, or status input as false," to assume "program take-up when required," and not to infer unlisted "benefit receipt." No prompt mentions TANF except to ask for the household's TANF amount, and none lists the non-cash benefit. PolicyEngine grants SNAP categorical eligibility to any household eligible for the non-cash benefit, without checking whether the household receives it. Among the {zeroAnswers} $0 answers, TANF appears in {zeroTanfMentions}, from Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the Texas resident.

The September 3 note counted {previousHouseholdCount} households at ${previousReference} each; PolicyBench now scores {householdCount} of them, at ${referenceAmount}. The ${previousReference} came from an unrounded minimum: ${previousMonthlyJanSep} a month through September and a projected ${previousMonthlyOctDec} from October. PolicyEngine has rounded the minimum to the nearest dollar since July 28 (#9162). PolicyBench no longer scores the other household, in Texas, because PolicyEngine computed its amount with {assumedHours} hours of work a week, which the prompt does not list. That note also said these states waive the asset test for households receiving the non-cash benefit; Texas keeps a ${bbceAssetLimitTx} asset limit, and PolicyEngine tests eligibility for the benefit, not receipt.
